Look, I get why the aggressive case sounds exciting. RSI 21, broken Bollinger band, historical oversold bounces of "double digits" — it's a compelling narrative. But my job isn't to find the most exciting narrative. It's to make sure the firm doesn't get carried out on a stretcher. Let me walk through why the arithmetic of A-share structure makes the aggressive framing dangerous, and why even the neutral "wait for the right side" position is too loose.

Start with the single fact the aggressive analyst keeps glossing over: **T+1 plus limit-down is not symmetric with T+1 plus limit-up.** He frames T+1 as a "help" because it locks in selling pressure and enables short squeezes. That's a story about the upside. But the structural asymmetry is that on the downside, T+1 removes your only real defense — the ability to exit intraday. If we buy at 1426 today and overnight we get a policy headline, a global risk-off session, or a batch-price scare, tomorrow's open can gap through our stop entirely. Our "ATR 35-45 yuan stop discipline" is a fiction in that scenario — the stop doesn't execute at the stop price, it executes wherever the market opens, possibly limit-down. On a limit-down day the buy side of the book is empty. The 15:05-15:30 fixed-price session exists since July 2026, yes, but it requires a counterparty, and on a limit-down day the counterparty is precisely what's missing. So the aggressive plan's entire risk control — "use position management to convert left-side risk into cost advantage" — rests on an exit that may not be available. That's not discipline. That's a plan that works in the 90% of days when nothing happens and fails catastrophically in the 10% when everything happens at once. For a conservative mandate, that tail is the whole ballgame.

Now the "four safety cushions" argument. Let me take them one at a time because they're doing a lot of work.

**Valuation cushion:** He says 20x PE with a 5% earnings yield in a 2.46% rate world is "bond-plus-option." But 20x PE is not a floor — it's a multiple that can compress. The fundamentals report is explicit: consensus has re-rated Moutai from growth to "stable value/bond-like" with ~6% EPS CAGR and PEG 3.35. If batch prices soften further or the mid-year report disappoints, the multiple goes to 17x, 15x. On a 1.64 trillion market cap, that's another 15-25% of downside with zero change in the business. "Cheap relative to history" is not the same as "cheap." And critically — a 5% earnings yield only protects you if you hold through the drawdown and collect it. Under a conservative mandate with mark-to-market and volatility constraints, a 20% drawdown is a real problem regardless of what the dividend yields.

**Supply cushion (zero lockup expiry):** I actually agree this is the one genuinely clean positive. But notice what it does and doesn't do. It removes one source of *new* supply. It does nothing about the existing supply — the institutions and northbound holders who are the ones actually selling. The lockup report itself says institutional de-risking is "normal secondary market activity, not lockup reduction." Right — and normal secondary market selling is exactly what produced the 9.28 billion... sorry, 9.28 *hundred million* northbound outflow and the 2.2x volume distribution day. Zero lockup expiry means no *additional* cliff. It is not a demand catalyst. The aggressive analyst is treating the absence of one negative as if it were the presence of a positive.

**Policy put:** Here I have to be blunt with both the aggressive and neutral analysts. The policy report says, in its own words, that it could not verify a single 2025 Q2 policy event — the news source returned dates from 2026, the individual-stock news returned zero results across every window. The aggressive analyst says "data missing is neutral, not negative" and then immediately treats the *hypothetical* consumption stimulus as a real +6-8% catalyst while treating the *hypothetical* consumption tax shift as a mere 25% probability footnote. That's asymmetric in exactly the wrong direction for a conservative book. If you're going to argue the policy put is real, you have to also argue the policy tax is real — and the tax is the one that hits earnings directly. A consumption tax shift to the wholesale/retail link compresses the channel, forces the company to cede margin to keep distributors whole, and even with Moutai's pricing power the policy report's own downside scenario is -8% to -12%. Probability-weighting that against an unverified stimulus upside and calling the net -1.5% "basically neutral" is fine for a research note. It is not a basis for adding risk into a broken chart.

**Sentiment extreme:** RSI 21 is the strongest card. But "oversold" is a condition, not a signal — the technical report is explicit that the RSI is *still falling*, no upward inflection, no bullish divergence, and the historical base rate for Moutai's RSI in the 40-70 range during healthy uptrends means 21 is genuinely extreme — which historically means *a bounce is likely at some point*, not that *today is the bottom*. Those are different claims. The aggressive plan buys 1426, 1390-1400, and 1350. That means he expects it can go to 1350 — a further 5.3% down — and he's fine with that because he's averaging. But averaging into a falling knife under T+1, where each tranche is locked the day you buy it and the gap risk is unhedgeable, means the firm's realized loss if the 1350 support fails is not the 5% he's modeling — it's whatever the gap delivers. And the report flags S3 at 1350 with nothing below it until much lower. The downside tail is open-ended.

Now the neutral position, "HOLD and wait for right-side confirmation." I want to be clear about why even this is too generous given our mandate. A HOLD is not free. We are carrying the position through a confirmed downtrend — broken 200-day, MACD accelerating below zero with no divergence, VWMA confirming volume-weighted distribution, closing at the day's low with no late-session support. The neutral analyst says "wait for RSI inflection plus volume contraction." Fine — but between now and then, we own the full downside of every overnight gap. The neutral position implicitly assumes the gap risk is symmetric because we're not adding. It isn't. We already hold the exposure. Holding through a distribution phase under T+1 is a decision to accept unprotected downside in exchange for... what, exactly? The option to sell higher later? That option costs us the gap risk every single night.

So here's the conservative conclusion, and it's not "HOLD."

The trader's reasoning actually contains the answer and then refuses to act on it. He says the technical picture proves this is "a real decline, not a washout," that left-side entry has poor risk-reward under T+1, that valuation offers no margin of safety at PEG 3.35, and that policy and batch-price data are missing so no directional judgment is possible. Every one of those points argues for *reducing* exposure, not maintaining it. If the thesis for owning the position is "downside protection from fundamentals and supply," and the market is telling you the downside protection is being tested right now with volume confirmation, the conservative response is to shrink the position to a size where a limit-down gap doesn't impair the portfolio, and re-enter only on the right-side signal the neutral analyst himself defined. That is: trim into strength if any appears above 1450-1485, cut further if 1425 fails on volume, and hold only a token core that we can afford to see gap.

The aggressive analyst says "missing the bottom is itself a risk." For a conservative mandate, that's backwards. Missing a bounce costs us opportunity. Being trapped in a limit-down gap with no exit costs us capital, and capital is the thing we're chartered to protect. The A-share structure — T+1 lock, limit-down order books that empty exactly when you need them, policy reversals that arrive overnight, hot money that leaves before retail knows — is specifically built so that the left-side buyer bears the unhedgeable tail. The aggressive plan works beautifully in the scenario where he's right and fails catastrophically in the scenario where he's wrong, and he cannot tell you which scenario he's in because the batch-price and policy data that would tell him are missing. That is the definition of a bet we should not be sizing up into.

So my counter to both of them: the aggressive analyst is buying a lottery ticket and calling it a cost advantage; the neutral analyst is holding a lottery ticket and calling it patience. Neither is protecting the firm. The correct conservative action is to reduce the position to a gap-tolerant core, set explicit trim triggers above 1450-1485 and below 1425, and refuse to add a single share until we have the two data points that actually determine the outcome — verified batch-price trend and the actual text of the consumption tax and stimulus documents — plus a right-side technical confirmation. That's not cowardice. That's the only position that survives the A-share structure when the overnight headline goes the wrong way.
